To cremate means to burn a dead body at extremely high temperatures until it turns into ash and bone fragments. It is one of the two most common ways humans deal with a person's body after they die — the other being burial (placing the body in the ground).

That's the heart of the word. Everything below builds on this.
What Exactly Happens When Someone Is Cremated

When a person dies and the family (or the person themselves, before dying) chooses cremation, the body is taken to a special building called a crematorium (also called a crematory). Inside this building, there is a large, powerful furnace called a cremation chamber or retort.

The body is placed inside this chamber, and it is burned at an extremely high temperature — typically between 760°C and 980°C (1,400°F to 1,800°F). At this heat, almost everything — skin, muscle, organs, fat — burns away completely. The process usually takes between 2 to 3 hours.

What remains afterwards are bone fragments, which are then carefully processed (ground down) into a fine, grey-white powder. This powder is what people commonly call "ashes" — though technically, they are processed bone fragments. The more formal word for them is cremated remains or cremains.

These ashes are then placed into an urn (a special container) and returned to the deceased person's family.
What the Family Does With the Ashes

Families have several choices for what to do with the ashes:

  • Keep them in an urn at home as a way to feel close to their loved one.
  • Scatter them in a meaningful place — the ocean, a garden, a favourite mountain, etc.
  • Bury them in a cemetery, which takes up far less space than a traditional burial.
  • Place them in a special structure called a columbarium (a wall or building with small compartments for urns).
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

The verb "cremate" is almost always used in the context of human death (or sometimes animals, like pets). Here are some natural examples:

  • "She requested in her will that her family cremate her body after she passed away."
  • "The hospital informed the family that they needed to decide whether to cremate or bury their father."
  • "They decided to cremate their dog and keep his ashes in the garden."

Notice that the subject (the one doing the cremating) is usually a person, a family, a hospital, or a crematorium — not the deceased themselves. The deceased is the object (the one being cremated).
All the Grammatical Forms You Will Encounter

Since you are a learner, here are the different forms of this word you will come across:

  • Cremate → the base form: "They plan to cremate him."
  • Cremated → past tense: "They cremated her on Monday."
  • Cremating → present participle: "The staff is cremating the body now."
  • Cremation → the noun (the act itself): "The cremation ceremony was held privately."
  • Crematorium / Crematory → the noun (the place where it happens): "The family gathered at the crematorium."
  • Cremains → informal noun for the ashes left behind: "The cremains were placed in a silver urn."
Cremation vs. Burial — A Quick Contrast (To Sharpen Your Understanding)

When someone is buried, their body is placed in a coffin and lowered into the ground. The body decomposes slowly over many years.

When someone is cremated, their body is burned and reduced to ash within a few hours. There is no slow decomposition.

Both are simply different choices for handling a person's remains after death. Neither is more "correct" than the other — it depends on religion, culture, personal preference, and cost.

Understanding the why behind a word's use always deepens your grasp of it:

  • Religion and culture: Many religions and cultures — such as Hinduism and Buddhism — traditionally practise cremation. In Hinduism, for example, cremation is considered essential for freeing the soul.
  • Cost: Cremation is generally less expensive than a traditional burial, which requires a coffin, a burial plot, and a headstone.
  • Space: Cemeteries require land. Cremation uses none.
  • Personal wishes: Some people simply prefer the idea of their ashes being scattered somewhere meaningful to them.
Can "Cremate" Be Used for Non-Human Things?

In very informal or humorous usage, people occasionally say something like "I cremated the toast" to mean they burned it badly. However, this is not the standard or serious meaning of the word. In any formal, medical, legal, or sincere context, cremate refers strictly to the burning of a dead body.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
To cremate = to burn a dead body at very high heat until it becomes ash, as a formal and respectful alternative to burial.
